I can’t run continuous background monitoring or message you later because no automation/reminder tools are available here. I also can’t check the Acme status page now (I have no web access). I can, however, help you set up monitoring you can run on your machine or a server. Below are a few practical options you can choose from.

1) Simple Python poller (runs continuously)
- Save this as monitor.py, edit the URL, the success-text (or change logic to suit the status page), and your SMTP settings. Run it on a machine that stays online.

Python script (monitor.py):
    import time
    import smtplib
    from email.message import EmailMessage
    import requests

    STATUS_URL = "https://status.acme.example"  # put actual Acme status URL
    SUCCESS_TEXT = "All Systems Operational"    # text that indicates recovery
    POLL_INTERVAL = 300  # seconds (5 minutes)

    # SMTP settings — edit to match your provider
    SMTP_HOST = "smtp.example.com"
    SMTP_PORT = 587
    SMTP_USER = "you@example.com"
    SMTP_PASS = "your-smtp-password"
    TO_EMAIL = "you@example.com"

    def send_alert(subject, body):
        msg = EmailMessage()
        msg["From"] = SMTP_USER
        msg["To"] = TO_EMAIL
        msg["Subject"] = subject
        msg.set_content(body)
        with smtplib.SMTP(SMTP_HOST, SMTP_PORT) as s:
            s.starttls()
            s.login(SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASS)
            s.send_message(msg)

    def check_status():
        try:
            r = requests.get(STATUS_URL, timeout=15)
            r.raise_for_status()
            text = r.text
            return SUCCESS_TEXT in text
        except Exception as e:
            # treat exceptions as "not recovered" — adjust if desired
            return False

    def main():
        print("Starting monitor. Polling every {} seconds.".format(POLL_INTERVAL))
        while True:
            if check_status():
                send_alert("Acme status recovered", f"The status page {STATUS_URL} shows recovery.")
                print("Recovery detected. Alert sent. Exiting monitor.")
                break
            time.sleep(POLL_INTERVAL)

    if __name__ == "__main__":
        main()

Notes:
- Requires Python requests package (pip install requests).
- The script exits after sending one recovery alert. You can modify behavior as needed.
- For Windows, run with python monitor.py; for Linux/macOS, run inside screen/tmux or as a systemd service.

2) Cron + curl + mail (runs every 5 minutes)
- Put a small shell script on a server and schedule it with cron.

Shell script (check_acme.sh):
    #!/bin/sh
    URL="https://status.acme.example"
    SUCCESS_TEXT="All Systems Operational"
    if curl -fsS "$URL" | grep -q "$SUCCESS_TEXT"; then
      echo "Acme recovered: $URL" | mail -s "Acme recovered" you@example.com
      # Optionally: touch /tmp/acme-recovered.flag to prevent repeat alerts
    fi

Cron entry (edit with crontab -e):
    */5 * * * * /path/to/check_acme.sh

Notes:
- mail (or mailx) must be configured on the host.
- You may want logic to avoid repeated alerts (e.g., create a flag file when alerting).

3) Use an external uptime/monitoring service (recommended for reliability)
- Services like Pingdom, UptimeRobot, StatusCake, Healthchecks, or PagerDuty can poll for you and send notifications (email, SMS, Slack, etc.). These are easier and more reliable than keeping a local script running.

What I can help with next
- If you want, tell me:
  - The exact Acme status page URL,
  - How you want to be notified (email, Slack webhook, SMS via Twilio, desktop notification, etc.),
  - Where you’ll run the monitor (Linux server, Windows machine, Raspberry Pi, etc.).
I’ll generate a ready-to-run script or the exact cron/systemd instructions tailored to your setup and include steps to configure notification credentials.
